module.title: Scope and Applicability of AI Systems

cues.text: All right. Welcome to this explainer for
module three. We are jumping right into
the absolute frontier of pharmaceutical
compliance today, defining the scope of
your AI systems under EU GMP Annex 22.
Look, if you're in pharma QA, IT, or
validation, you already know the drill.
Getting your arms around what actually
counts as AI and exactly how strictly it
needs to be governed, well, it's pretty
much one of the biggest challenges we're
facing right now. So, let's get into it.
So, here's our road map for this module.
We're going to cover the high stakes of
scoping, the decision funnel,
classifying risk tiers, static versus
dynamic models, some complex boundary
cases, and finally, building that
defensible inventory. Let's hit the
road. Starting off with section one, the
high stakes of scoping. Because, make no
mistake, your scope decisions literally
drive every downstream governance
action. Think about it. If you
defensively over claim, meaning, you
know, you just throw every single piece
of conventional software into the Annex
22 bucket just to play it safe, you're
going to absolutely paralyze your
validation team with wasted effort. But,
on the flip side, if you defensively
under claim and miss some sneaky little
AI system operating in a regulated
space, boom, you are essentially handing
an inspector a free finding. We really
need to find that disciplined middle
ground here.
To find that middle ground, we use a
strict decision funnel. I like to think
of this like a bouncer at an exclusive
club. Every piece of software, every
algorithm, has to pass these exact five
steps to determine its Annex 22 fate. We
ask, is it AI? We check its GMP impact,
classify the risk tier, analyze its
architecture, and finally, document it.
Which brings us to step one. Is it
actually AI? We all know a lot of
software vendors will just slap an AI
label on their product to make a quick
sale, right? But, listen, traditional
rule-based logic, expert systems, and
deterministic algorithms, those stay
safely under standard Annex 11
governance. No Annex 22 needed. It's
only when a system actually uses
statistical learning, pattern
recognition, or generative AI to produce
decisions or recommendations that it
crosses the threshold. That's your
trigger.
Okay, so let's say it is true AI. We
move to the next filter in our funnel
and we have to ask the million-dollar
question. Does it actually have a good
manufacturing practice impact? Now, this
goes way beyond just direct
manufacturing control or batch release.
Yes, obviously AI-supported spec setting
or automated deviation classifications
are clearly in scope, but you really
have to look at indirect effects, too.
For example, say you're using an AI
scheduling tool that determines the
availability of qualified personnel on
the floor. Or an AI that optimizes
training and affects operator competency
tracking. Well, that indirect effect
absolutely warrants Annex 22 scrutiny.
Bottom line, if it touches the quality
system, it's in.
>> Moving to section three, classifying AI
risk tiers.
>> This four-tier matrix is exactly the
mental model your QA team needs to
adopt. At the very top, we have
unacceptable. Things like continuously
learning AI making autonomous batch
release decisions. Annex 22 strictly
absolutely excludes that. Right below
that is high risk, like static AI
driving process analytical technology,
which requires full-blown validation.
Then there's moderate risk for AI
decision support, like deviation triage,
but only assuming humans are actively
reviewing the output before taking
action. And finally, low risk handles
all those non-GMP back office
administrative tasks.
Next up, step four, static versus
dynamic models.
So, Annex 22 heavily, heavily favors
static models. These are models that are
effectively frozen in time after
validation. The outputs are
deterministic, they're reproducible, and
updates only ever happen by a formal
change control. Because they are audit
defensible across time, they're
permitted for critical GMP processes.
Dynamic models, on the other hand, they
are continuously learning from
operational data. They can literally
drift between batches. Because they are
so notoriously difficult to qualify and
audit, they are heavily restricted and
frankly outright excluded for critical
GMP decisions without some extraordinary
justification. And then, of course, we
have generative AI like your large
language models. Because gen AI can, you
know, confidently hallucinate incorrect
outputs, spitting out data that looks
highly plausible but is just completely
wrong, you absolutely cannot use it for
critical tasks like specification
setting. No way. However, it is
acceptable for assistive use like
drafting documents, just as long as a
qualified human actively reviews and
verifies the content before it ever
becomes a formal GMP record.
Let's put this into practice with
section five, navigating complex
boundary cases.
In our first scenario, imagine a
pharmaceutical filler considering a deep
learning particulate inspection system.
This system grades vials as clear
passes, clear fails, or it kicks them
out for manual human review.
Now, initially, the filler tries to
classify this AI as just moderate risk
because, hey, humans are reviewing the
borderline vials, right? Makes sense on
paper.
But, here is the catch. The system is
performing final pass or fail
classification on the vast majority of
those vials completely autonomously. An
inspector is going to immediately
escalate this to high risk. The big
lesson here is that autonomous decision
rates dictate the rules. Just having
partial oversight on the tricky cases
does not magically lower your overall
risk tier. To actually resolve this, you
need full validation, drift monitoring,
and an explicit fallback to fully manual
inspection if the AI starts to drift.
Next up, let's look at generative AI
document drafting. Say a QA team wants
to deploy an LLM to take some rough
operator notes and turn them into highly
polished deviation reports. A lot of
teams dangerously assume this is
automatically a low-risk application
just because a human QA reviewer
eventually signs off on that final
draft. And this perfectly illustrates a
really common trap. The issue is that
the AI subtly shapes the framing of the
event, the root cause hypotheses, and
even the CAPA suggestions. If your
humans are just passively spell-checking
and approving these beautifully written
drafts, you have massive moderate risk
exposure. To keep this compliant, you
have to prove to an inspector that your
reviewers are trained to actively
challenge the AI's logic. Honestly, you
should probably be tracking metrics on
how often the AI text is actually
altered during that review process.
Finally, consider the trap of using a
third-party cloud-based AI tool. Let's
say a lab is using a vendor's AI service
via API for assay data analysis. In this
case, the vendor completely controls the
black box model, the training data, and
the entire update cycle.
The harsh reality here is you cannot
outsource your GMP accountability. If
you don't control the algorithm, and you
literally can't validate the vendor's
continuous background updates, you're
accountable for behavior you cannot
document. So, the resolution? You
absolutely must treat this AI strictly
as an advisory tool. You have to perform
a duplicate analysis using your own
in-house validated methods, and just use
the cloud AI as a secondary check, never
your primary decision maker.
Which brings us to our final section,
the defensible AI inventory.
This inventory is a living document, and
it has to contain these exact attributes
for every single system. The identifier,
its intended use, its specific risk
tier, the system owner, its validation
status, and probably most importantly, a
direct link to your documented scoping
rationale.
This is your master index. When an
auditor walks through the door and says,
"Show me your AI systems," this document
is your absolute best line of defense.
I really love this quote from the source
material. Strong scoping discipline
projects competence and reduces the
inspector's incentive to probe deeper.
An inspector will instantly sense if
your inventory was just hastily thrown
together or if it's outdated. But a
meticulously documented log, especially
one that details exactly why certain
boundary cases were classified the way
they were, that proves your
organizational maturity. It shows you're
in total control, which naturally
reduces the inspector's urge to just dig
endlessly into your portfolio.
So, I'm going to leave you with this
final thought to evaluate with your own
IT, QA, and validation teams. Could your
current AI inventory actually withstand
that level of regulatory scrutiny today?
Are you over claiming, under claiming,
or you perfectly scoped? Take these
concepts back to your organization, chew
on them a bit, and we'll see you in

proportionate governance and validation
strategies. Thanks for joining me.
